# Four Positions on Open-Source AI Regulation

---

## 1. Completely Open

**Steelman:**
The strongest case for fully open AI development rests on three pillars. First, **collective scrutiny beats closed-door development**—open weights allow thousands of researchers to find vulnerabilities, test alignment, and improve safety in ways that no single corporation can accomplish alone. Second, **the diffusion of power matters**: if only a handful of large companies control AI, they become unaccountable infrastructure with incentives toward monopolization. Third, **capabilities are already widespread**—the underlying research is in papers, the compute exists, and talented researchers can replicate results. Restriction would only hobble legitimate actors while bad actors proceed anyway, leaving us with the worst of both worlds: no safety benefits but concentrated power.

**Typical Counter-Argument:**
This position underestimates **asymmetric risk**. A single malicious actor using an open powerful model can cause disproportionate harm—synthesizing bioweapons, running sophisticated influence ops, automating cyberattacks—while defenders must succeed every time. The "many eyes" argument assumes all eyes are benevolent or competent, but adversarial exploitation requires only one breakthrough, not collective vigilance. Furthermore, alignment research is not advanced by releasing capable but unaligned systems.

**Historical Analogy:**
The **early internet and World Wide Web (1990s–2000s)**. Tim Berners-Lee deliberately refused to patent his protocols, enabling explosive innovation. The web was largely unregulated, and while spam, malware, and fraud proliferated, the net economic and social benefit was enormous. Critics called for heavy regulation; proponents argued openness enabled resilience and that threats could be addressed selectively
